newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Brown pledges job creation, no tax rises.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Brown pledges job creation, no tax rises.

text.p: Opposition finance spokesman Gordon Brown said on Wednesday that a Labour government would increase spending on the National Health Service (NHS) by more than the rate of inflation.
Brown's pledge matched one made by the ruling Conservatives last October which his Labour Party, wary of making high-spending promises, had previously declined to match.

"We will give the NHS more money every year, but unlike the Tories (Conservatives) we will insist that every penny of that goes not to administration but to patient care," Brown told a meeting in Basildon, east of London.
The Conservatives accused Labour of making a policy U-turn.
"Mr Brown and Mr (Labour leader Tony) Blair have always refused to match this pledge, now they recognise they have lost the argument," health minister Stephen Dorrell said.
Brown also pledged to put job creation at the centre of his party's policies but said he would not raise income tax rates to fund them.
He said government investment was needed to create jobs, particularly for the young, and a windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities would provide the funds.

"Because I want to encourage and reward work, the basic and top rate (of income tax) will remain unchanged," he said. "And because I want to reward work especially for the low paid, we will introduce, when we can, a 10 pence starting rate of tax."
But there would be no free ride for the unemployed, he said -- no option of a life permanently on benefit.

Labour on Wednesday agreed a tax-cutting manifesto, pledging not to increase income tax rates for the full five years of a Labour government and to cut Value Added Tax on heating from eight to five percent. It also highlighted its "ambition" to cut the starting rate of income tax to 10 percent from 20.
The election is set for May 1 and Labour, riding high in the polls, is in prime position to take power.
Labour's jobs scheme extended beyond just tax and investment to the education system, Brown said.

"Our future starts with education, not from decisions we make today in Britain's boardrooms, but from what we do in Britain's classrooms," he said, pledging to pay for smaller classes in state schools.
Brown confirmed that a national minimum wage, attacked by the Conservatives as a policy that would cost jobs, would be introduced.
"The Tories are simply wrong to claim that Labour's minimum wage would kill jobs. Labour's minimum wage is a vital component of a strategy that will create jobs."
